turns.prompt_text: I have many jpeg images of writings I've written in cursive, I would like to mass ocr them to text
turns.response_html:
Standard Optical Character Recognition (OCR) often fails with cursive because it looks for separated, printed block letters. For cursive, you need Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR).

Since you have "many" images and want to "mass" process them, you likely need a solution that avoids opening files one by one. Below are the best methods ranging from user-friendly apps to powerful developer tools.

1. The "Pro" Archival Choice: Transkribus

This is the gold standard for historians and archivists. It is specifically designed to read difficult handwriting (even historical scripts).

  • How it works: You upload your images to their platform. You can use their public AI models, but the "killer feature" is that you can train a model on your own handwriting. By transcribing ~20-50 pages manually, the AI learns your specific cursive style and can auto-process the rest with high accuracy.
  • Cost: Uses a credit system (freemium). You get roughly 500 pages free upon sign-up, which might cover your batch.
  • Best for: High accuracy and large projects where you want the computer to "learn" your writing style.

2. The "Modern" AI Route: LLMs (ChatGPT / Gemini)

Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro are surprisingly excellent at reading messy handwriting because they understand context (they guess the word based on the sentence, not just the shape).

  • How to do it:
    • Manual Batch: If you have a subscription (ChatGPT Plus or Gemini Advanced), you can upload 10-20 JPEGs at a time and ask it to "Transcribe these handwritten notes verbatim into a single text block."
    • Pros: Extremely high accuracy; handles messy layouts well.
    • Cons: Privacy (your data goes to the model provider); file upload limits per chat.

3. The "Free" Batch Hack: Google Drive (Requires light scripting)

Google Drive has one of the best handwriting OCR engines in the world built-in for free, but it doesn't have a "batch" button by default.

  • The Manual Trick: If you upload a JPEG to Drive, right-click it, and select Open with > Google Docs, it will automatically convert the image to text.
  • The Mass Automation: You can automate this for hundreds of files using a simple Google Apps Script.
    1. Upload all JPEGs to a specific Google Drive folder.
    2. Open a Google Sheet, go to Extensions > Apps Script.
    3. Use a script that iterates through that folder, converts each image to a Doc, extracts the text body, and appends it to your Sheet. (I can provide this script if you are comfortable pasting code).

4. The "No-Code" App: Pen to Print

If you prefer a paid app that just works out of the box without technical setup.

  • Platform: Mobile (iOS/Android) with a Web interface.
  • Workflow: It is designed specifically for cursive. You can export the text to a text file or PDF.
  • Cons: The "Batch" export features usually require a premium subscription, and it is often more mobile-focused (scanning via camera) than bulk-import focused, though the web plan allows file uploads.

5. The Developer Route (Python + Cloud Vision)

If you are comfortable running a Python script on your computer, this is the most robust and cheapest "mass" method.

  • Tools: Google Cloud Vision API, AWS Textract, or Azure Computer Vision.
  • Why: These APIs charge pennies per 1,000 images (often with a free tier for the first 1,000/month). They are what the "Pro" apps use under the hood.
  • Workflow: You put all JPEGs in a folder, run a script, and it outputs a .txt file for every image.

Recommendation

  • If you want the highest accuracy and have >100 pages: Use Transkribus. It is worth the learning curve.
  • If you want a quick, free, slightly "hacky" solution: Use the Google Drive method (I can write the script for you).
  • If you want ease of use and don't mind paying: Look at Pen to Print.

Would you like me to write the Google Apps Script for you to batch-process these in Drive?
